conclusion.justification: The report notes that evidence is mixed and has shifted toward uncertainty or no benefit, highlighting that the highest-quality recent trials and updated Cochrane review show no significant reduction in diarrhea duration or treat the benefit as uncertain/absent.
conclusion.label: leans_reject

report:
**Conclusion:** The evidence on probiotics for acute infectious diarrhea is mixed and has shifted over time toward uncertainty/no benefit, especially in high-quality trials.

Older meta-analyses (e.g., Allen et al., Lancet, and earlier Cochrane versions) suggested probiotics modestly shortened diarrhea duration, particularly in children. However, the most authoritative and recent synthesis—the 2020 Cochrane systematic review (Collinson et al., updated from Allen 2003/2010)—substantially revised this conclusion. After incorporating newer, larger, more rigorous trials, the review authors found it **uncertain whether probiotics affect diarrhea duration**, and noted that overall confidence in earlier positive findings was undermined by inclusion of higher-quality studies showing no benefit (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8166250/; https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea). A commentary on this update states plainly: "There is no evidence that probiotics are effective in treating acute infectious diarrhoea," reversing prior editions' favorable conclusions (https://www.evidence4health.org/news-events/news/updated-cochrane-review-on-probiotics-for-treating-acute-infectious-diarrhoea.html).

This shift is corroborated by two large, well-designed pediatric emergency department RCTs (including the 2018 NEJM trial of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG) that found **no significant reduction** in diarrhea duration or severity compared to placebo—these trials heavily influenced the Cochrane update (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802598).

Some newer meta-analyses in children (2023–2025, e.g., Frontiers, ScienceDirect) still report modest benefits, but rate certainty of evidence as "very low," and clinical guidance bodies note effects are inconsistent across strains and populations.

**Bottom line:** Probiotics may modestly shorten diarrhea in some populations (especially children), but the highest-quality, most recent evidence (2020 Cochrane review, large RCTs) indicates the benefit is uncertain or absent, and routine use is not currently recommended based on rigorous trial data.
